title: Tteok Guk
subtitle: New Year rice cake soup in clear beef broth
excerpt: Oval rice cake coins are simmered in a clear beef broth until tender, then finished with shredded beef, ribbons of thin omelette and nori strips. This recipe serves 4 and takes around 40 minutes. Tteok guk is the soup eaten on Lunar New Year morning across Korea, and the tradition holds that each bowl consumed means you have aged a year.
sourceNotes: Tteok guk has been the canonical Lunar New Year food in Korea for centuries. The white oval rice cakes symbolise purity and new beginnings, and the round shape echoes old Korean coins, representing prosperity for the year ahead. The dish is mentioned in Joseon dynasty records and has remained unchanged in form and meaning.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the beef broth a day ahead and refrigerate. Skim the fat from the surface before reheating. Add the rice cakes only when ready to serve.

glossaryTerms.definition: Tteok guk is the soup eaten on the morning of Korean Lunar New Year (Seollal). The name combines tteok (rice cake) and guk (soup). Eating a bowl is said to symbolically add a year to your age, which is why Koreans sometimes ask 'have you eaten your tteok guk yet?' as a way of asking whether someone has celebrated the new year. The soup must be made with the oval-sliced white rice cakes rather than any other tteok variety.

Tteok is the Korean term for rice cake, made by pounding or pressing cooked glutinous or short-grain rice into a dense, chewy mass. There are hundreds of varieties of tteok in Korean cuisine, used in savoury dishes and sweet confections alike. For tteok guk, the garae-tteok variety is used: long cylindrical white rice cakes sliced into oval coins on the diagonal. They are available in Asian supermarkets, fresh or vacuum-packed.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes around 40 minutes from start to finish.
is built on a clean beef broth, and the oval
coins are added only at the end so they remain chewy rather than dissolving into the broth. The garnishes turn a simple soup into something visually striking.

Soak the rice cakes in cold water for 20 minutes before using if they are refrigerated or vacuum-packed. This softens them slightly so they cook more evenly in the broth and do not go too stodgy. Do not add them to the soup too early or they will over-soften and lose their texture.

items.prepNote: sliced into oval coins on the diagonal, soaked in cold water for 20 minutes
kept in one piece for the broth, then shredded
cut into thin strips for garnish

content.text: Place the beef in a large saucepan with the water. Bring to the boil, skim any foam, then reduce to a simmer. Cook for 15 minutes until the beef is cooked through.
Lift out the beef and set aside to cool. Add the garlic and soy sauce to the broth. Simmer for 5 more minutes.

Make the egg garnish. Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt. Heat a lightly oiled small frying pan over a low heat and pour in the egg to make a thin omelette. Cook for 1 minute, flip, cook for 30 seconds, then slide out and cut into thin strips.
Shred the cooled beef into thin pieces with your fingers or two forks.
Drain the soaked rice cakes and add them to the simmering broth. Cook for 4 to 5 minutes until tender but still slightly chewy. Add the spring onions in the final minute.
Season with salt, then stir in the sesame oil. Ladle into bowls and top each with shredded beef, egg strips and nori strips. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: Rice cakes have dissolved and turned to mush
items.cause: They were added too early or cooked for too long
items.fix: Add the rice cakes only in the final 5 minutes of cooking and taste one at 4 minutes. They should be soft all the way through but still have a slight chew. Remove from the heat as soon as they are done.

items.symptom: Rice cakes are sticking together in a clump
items.cause: They were not soaked before being added, or were added to the pot all at once
items.fix: Soak the rice cakes in cold water for 20 minutes before using to separate them. Stir the soup gently as you add them to the pot so each piece goes in separately.

items.symptom: Broth is dark and strong rather than light and clear
items.cause: Too much soy sauce was added
items.fix: Add soy sauce in small increments and taste as you go. The broth should be a pale golden colour with a gentle savoury flavour. Dilute with a little water if it has gone too dark.

content.text: Tteok guk is as embedded in Korean culture as any dish can be. On the morning of Seollal, the Korean Lunar New Year, it appears on tables across the country before any other food. Families gather, the soup is served, and the new year begins. The white rice cakes symbolise a clean start. The oval shape echoes old coins and speaks to the hope for prosperity. It is a simple soup in its ingredients but carries the weight of an entire cultural tradition.
